common_name: Pretty, Tasty Ruby Strawberry (Ornamental Clumping Everbearing Strawberry)

planting.note: Set divisions or plugs out after the last frost, or in early fall in mild climates, so the clumping crown establishes before heavy bloom.

directions: Pretty, Tasty Ruby is an ornamental-edible strawberry bred for display as much as for fruit, producing rose-like double red flowers continuously above sturdy foliage for months. Because it forms a tight clump with very few runners, it stays tidy in hanging baskets, strawberry pots, and front-of-border plantings instead of sprawling. Grow in full sun to part shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, and expect abundant clusters of medium red berries alongside the ongoing bloom. Deadhead spent flower clusters occasionally to keep new buds coming through the warm season.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring or early fall; establishes as a dense mat within one growing season.

directions: NOVA White bugleweed forms a glossy, forest-green evergreen mat studded with abundant icicle-like white flower spikes through June and July. Its spreading, non-invasive habit makes it useful as a groundcover, edging plant, or shade-tolerant filler between stepping stones. Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil from full sun to full shade, with average water; part shade gives the densest foliage and best flowering. Shear lightly after bloom to tidy the mat and encourage fresh growth.

common_name: Rocky's Eye Daylily (Lavender Pink with Purple Eyezone)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rocky's Eye is a dormant diploid daylily later used as a breeding parent of Tim Herrington's 1996 introduction 'Baby Boomer.'

directions: Registered by Heather Herrington in 1992, Rocky's Eye is a dormant diploid daylily bearing lavender-pink flowers about 4.25 inches across marked with a purple eyezone above a green throat, carried on 24-inch scapes that open early to midseason with rebloom. Beyond its own garden merit, it was later used as a parent, crossed into a seedling line, behind Tim Herrington's 1996 introduction 'Baby Boomer.' Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Daggy Daylily (Yellow Ochre with Dark Red Eyezone)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Daggy is an evergreen diploid daylily bred from 'Enchanter's Spell' x 'Baby Fresh' and later used as a parent of Tim Herrington's 1996 introduction 'Baby Boomer.'

directions: Registered by E.R. (Enman) Joiner in 1993 from a cross of 'Enchanter's Spell' and 'Baby Fresh', Daggy is an evergreen diploid daylily with yellow-ochre flowers about 3.5 inches across marked with a dark red eyezone above a green throat, carried on 20-inch scapes that open early with rebloom. It was later used as a parent, crossed into a seedling line, behind Tim Herrington's 1996 introduction 'Baby Boomer.' Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Malvaticum Azalea (Early Kurume Breeding Parent, Registered 1910)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Malvaticum is an obtusum-type (Kurume) azalea registered in 1910, grown today chiefly for its place in azalea breeding history.

directions: Malvaticum is an early Rhododendron obtusum (Kurume) azalea registered in 1910, significant today chiefly as a breeding parent rather than as a documented garden plant in its own right. Crossed with 'Suetsumu', it produced the celebrated Dutch introduction 'Addy Wery.' No reliable record of Malvaticum's own flower color, size, or original hybridizer survives in the sources consulted, a common gap for early Kurume parent clones overshadowed by their famous offspring. Grow it, as with other Kurume-type azaleas, in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, pruning only right after bloom since next year's flower buds form soon afterward.

common_name: Kokoku Satsuki Azalea (White and Pink, 1939 Gumpo x Fujinami Cross)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Kokoku was registered in Japan in 1939 from a cross of 'Gumpo' and 'Fujinami'.

directions: Kokoku (皇国) is a Japanese Satsuki azalea registered in 1939 from a cross of the seed parent 'Gumpo' and pollen parent 'Fujinami', bearing average-sized flowers in white overlaid with pink secondary markings. Like other Satsuki selections it flowers later in the season than Kurume or Southern Indica azaleas, so prune only right after bloom finishes since next year's flower buds set soon afterward. Grow in acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, and protect from hot afternoon sun which can scorch the foliage.
